The roof coverings appear to have been replaced or re-covered at some point in the past, although the exact date could not be established. It is likely that the original roof covering comprised clay or slate tiles. The current interlocking concrete tiles are considerably heavier than traditional clay or slate tiles, which can result in overloading of the roof timbers. However, where visible, there were no excessive signs of deflection or distortion to the roof structure. That said, shakes were observed in some timbers, and additional strutting supports have been provided, suggesting the roof has experienced some minor movement in the past. Your legal adviser should confirm whether Building Regulations approval was obtained for these alterations (see more comments in Sections E1 and H1).

Where partially visible, we observed that the underfelt at the edges of the roof on the two-storey rear addition is not correctly lapped into the gutter. The primary function of roofing underfelt is to provide an additional layer of protection against water penetration. Properly lapping the felt into the rainwater gutter ensures that any water that gets beneath the roof tiles is directed into the gutter, preventing it from running down the fascia or into the building structure. If the roofing felt is not properly lapped into the gutter, water could potentially seep behind the gutter or into the wall structure, leading to dampness, rot, or other moisture-related issues. The underfelt should extend beyond the edge of the roof and into the gutter to ensure that water flows directly into the gutter. Further investigation by a competent roofing contractor is recommended to carry out the necessary repairs and ensure the roof coverings are fully watertight. Additionally, the condition of the roof timbers at the edges of the roof should be checked to ensure there is no rot.

The roof is of butterfly construction, and roof coverings could not be inspected in this area due to no available vantage point.

There is evidence of cracking of the rear roof verge and there is some moss and lichen growth on the roof, which should be removed periodically. Moss and lichen can inhibit the roof’s efficiency by trapping moisture, which can lead to the deterioration of roof materials over time. Additionally, the build-up of moss can cause blockages in gutters and rainwater goods, impeding the proper drainage of rainwater and increasing the risk of water ingress into the property.

Velux-type roof lights have been installed. Detailed inspection of these areas was not feasible due to limited access, and our examination was restricted to visual inspection from inside the property and outside using binoculars. It is crucial to ensure that the flashing detail surrounding these roof lights is in good condition, as any failure could allow dampness to enter the property, leading to significant deterioration of the roof timbers. Generally, approval under the Building Regulations is required for the installation of a new roof light. Whilst our understanding is that the installation of roof lights typically does not necessitate planning permission, it is essential for your legal adviser to confirm this understanding (see Section H1). Where visible, no significant defects were noted.

The property has solar panels installed (photovoltaic). We have not inspected or tested the panels and you should arrange for an inspection by a specialist. It should be confirmed by your legal adviser the Photovoltaic panels fitted to this property are wholly owned by the vendor or are leased under a lender approved scheme (see Section I).

D4 – Main walls

We have assumed during our inspection that no deleterious or hazardous materials or techniques have been used, and the inspection of those parts which cannot be seen would not reveal material deficiencies or defects. No hazardous material was noted.

There is a history of underpinning to the property. It should be noted that different lenders may have different policies and approaches towards properties with history of underpinning. Your legal adviser should investigate and request the relevant documentation for the works that have been undertaken and ensure all remedial work is carried out under a long term and meaningful guarantee with a suitable insurance indemnity. It is imperative that the relevant documentation for this is requested to include Building Regulations approval.

We could not confirm whether the building contains reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC). As the building is of concrete frame construction with concrete elements in various locations, there is a possibility that this material may be present. We are not specialists and have not undertaken any intrusive investigations or specialist tests. Your solicitor should make further enquiries with the building management as to this matter. If RAAC has been or is identified, this is likely to have a large impact on the future saleability of the property and more importantly on the health and safety of the occupiers of the building. You should ask your legal adviser about this and also check with the building management to confirm if adequate and valid building insurance is in place to include any future defects arising as a result of the potential presence of this material.

We noted masonry bees. There are holes in the external walls, typical of those produced by masonry bees, which can cause substantial erosion and weakness of the joints. In severe cases this can affect the stability of the walling. The situation should be checked during the summer period when the bees are active and if these are seen entering the wall structure, the advice of the Environmental Health Officer of the Local Authority should be sought.

The small beam that spans across the top of openings in the masonry (lintel) has a defect and is cracked. This should be repaired soon. To repair the lintel properly it may have to be replaced completely.

A crack to the front bay has been noted, requiring repair by strengthening the masonry fabric and resin injection repairs. Regarding repair of the cracks, this involves strengthening the external wall cracks with the installation of ‘Helifix’ bars and resin injection repairs. This consists of 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars inserted into the bed joints at approximately 500 mm each side of the crack. The bars are inserted every 2–3 courses of brick. The cracks in the bricks can either be replaced or resin grouted with low viscosity grout such as ‘Nitokit LV’ by Fosroc. A well-installed ‘Helifix’ bar repair should blend into the façade and not be visibly prominent. If further movement is noticed after repairs are undertaken, the lintel will need to be either replaced or strengthened (by providing a steel plate to the underside of the masonry or similar). Replacement of the lintel will require Building Regulations approval.
